title: The Constitution of India — An Introduction
summary: Every year on 26 January, India celebrates Republic Day to mark the day its Constitution came into effect in 1950. But what is a constitution, and why does a country need one? This chapter explains that a constitution is the supreme 'rulebook' of a nation — a document that spells out the basic principles and laws, sets up the three organs of government (legislature, executive and judiciary), arranges checks and balances among them, lists the rights and duties of citizens, and states the long-term goals and values of the country. It tells the story of how India's Constitution was written by a Constituent Assembly formed in 1946 (389 members, later 299 after Partition, including 15 women), chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, with a Drafting Committee headed by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, and adopted on 26 November 1949. It traces the three great influences on the Constitution — the freedom struggle, India's civilisational heritage, and useful learnings from other countries' constitutions. It introduces the Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles of State Policy, explains why the Constitution is a 'living document' that can be amended, and unpacks the nine key words of the Preamble — Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic, Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.

topics.title: What Is a Constitution and Why We Need One
topics.summary: The idea of a constitution as a country's rulebook, the four big things it lays down, why a shared rulebook everyone agrees to is essential, and why high officials pledge to uphold it.

concepts.title: What a Constitution Is

explanations.oneLine: A constitution is the document that spells out a nation's basic principles and laws.
explanations.kidFriendly: Think of a constitution as the master rulebook of a whole country. It says what kind of government the country will have, how that government is formed, what powers each part has, and what rights and duties the people have. India's Constitution is so important that it is kept safe in a special helium-filled glass case in Parliament so it does not get damaged over time.
explanations.textbook: A constitution is a document that spells out a nation's basic principles and laws. It lays out four main things: (1) the framework of the three organs of the government — the legislature, the executive and the judiciary — and their roles and responsibilities; (2) the checks and balances among these three organs to ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability; (3) the rights and duties of the citizens; and (4) an outline of the long-term goals and aspirations of the nation. Many constitutions, including India's, also state the values and ideals the country is committed to, such as equality, justice, fraternity, pluralism and freedom.
explanations.expert: A constitution is the supreme, foundational law of a state — the law from which all other laws derive their authority and against which they are tested for validity. Analytically it does two distinct jobs: it is 'constitutive' (it creates and empowers the organs of government, defining and limiting their jurisdiction) and it is 'aspirational' (it declares the values and long-term goals the polity commits to). Because it sits above ordinary legislation, a constitution typically also fixes the special procedure by which it alone can be changed. The blend of a power-distributing framework, an enforceable charter of rights, and a statement of guiding ideals is what distinguishes a constitution from a mere collection of statutes.

concepts.reasoning: A country is made of millions of people, many institutions and competing interests. To function fairly, everyone must agree in advance on one supreme set of rules: who governs, how, with what limits, and with what protections for individuals. A constitution is exactly that agreed, written foundation, which is why it ranks above every ordinary law.

concepts.title: Why We Need a Constitution

explanations.oneLine: We need a constitution so that everyone agrees in advance on fair rules for running the country and settling disputes.
explanations.kidFriendly: Imagine a big kabaddi match with no rulebook. When a dispute breaks out, there is no fair way to settle it — each side just argues louder! A rulebook that both teams accept lets the referee settle things peacefully. A constitution is the 'rulebook' for a whole country: because everyone agrees to follow it, arguments about power and rights can be settled fairly instead of by force.
explanations.textbook: The chapter explains the need for a constitution with the example of a kabaddi match: when a dispute arises, the referee and captains turn to an official rulebook that everyone has agreed to follow, and the dispute is settled fairly. Without such a rulebook, or if a team refused to accept it, there would be no fair way to resolve the disagreement. A constitution works the same way for a country. Its basic rules and principles determine what kind of government there will be, how it will be formed and how it will function — how laws are made and implemented, who elects the executive, how the judiciary is set up, and what rights and duties citizens have. Because everyone agrees to abide by it, the constitution lets a large, diverse country be governed fairly and peacefully.
explanations.expert: The need for a constitution rests on the problem of legitimacy and coordination in a large society. Power must be exercised, but for it to be accepted rather than merely obeyed under threat, it must flow from rules agreed in advance and applied impartially. A constitution supplies this 'pre-commitment': by binding even the government to higher rules, it converts raw power into lawful authority, makes outcomes predictable, and provides a neutral standard (interpreted by an independent judiciary) for resolving disputes. The kabaddi analogy captures the deeper point — rules are useful only if the players accept their authority; a constitution must therefore command broad consent, which is why India's was made by a representative assembly rather than imposed by a ruler.

concepts.reasoning: Disputes are inevitable wherever people share power and resources. If there is no agreed, written standard to appeal to, disputes are settled by whoever is stronger or louder. A constitution gives everyone — including the government — a common rulebook they have promised to follow, so disagreements can be settled fairly and the same way every time.

whyChain: Why does a country need a constitution at all? Because a country is made of millions of people, many institutions, and groups with very different interests. Whenever power and resources are shared, disagreements are certain to arise. Without a single agreed set of rules to turn to, every dispute would be settled by whoever is stronger, richer or louder, which is neither fair nor peaceful. A constitution provides one supreme rulebook that everyone, including the government, has promised to follow.

Why does writing the rules down and agreeing to them in advance help? Because rules fixed beforehand are predictable and neutral — they do not bend to favour the powerful in the heat of a quarrel. In the kabaddi example, the referee and captains settle the dispute calmly by reading a rulebook both sides already accepted. In the same way, when citizens and the government accept the constitution ahead of time, conflicts about power, elections or rights can be decided by a known standard rather than by force or shouting.

Why must even the rulers be bound by it? Because if the people who hold power could ignore the rules, the rulebook would protect no one. By binding the president, prime minister, ministers and judges — all of whom pledge to uphold it — the constitution turns raw power into lawful authority that the people can trust and question. This is exactly why India's Constitution was written by a representative Constituent Assembly and not handed down by a king: rules command real obedience only when people accept their authority as their own.

concepts.title: Officials Who Pledge to Uphold the Constitution

explanations.oneLine: Key officials such as the President, Prime Minister, ministers and judges take an oath to follow and protect the Constitution.
explanations.kidFriendly: The Constitution is not just a book on a shelf — the most powerful people in the country promise to obey it. The President takes an oath to 'preserve, protect, and defend' the Constitution, and the Prime Minister, the ministers and the judges all promise to follow its rules. So even the highest leaders are bound by the same rulebook.
explanations.textbook: The Constitution of India is the document that many of the country's important officials pledge to uphold. The President takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend it. The Prime Minister, the council of ministers, and the judges promise to follow its provisions. This means that the people who hold the greatest power in the country are themselves bound by the Constitution and must act according to its rules.
explanations.expert: The oath of office is the mechanism that converts a written constitution into binding practice. By swearing to uphold the Constitution, office-holders accept that their authority is conditional and limited — they may act only within the powers the Constitution grants and must defend the document itself against violation. This is the practical face of constitutionalism: the principle that government is subordinate to, not the master of, the supreme law. The President's specific duty to 'preserve, protect and defend' the Constitution makes the head of state its ultimate guardian, while the obligation on judges underpins judicial review, the power to test ordinary laws and executive actions against the Constitution and strike down those that conflict with it.

concepts.reasoning: A rulebook only works if those with power agree to be bound by it. By taking a public oath, the country's highest officials accept that their authority comes from the Constitution and is limited by it — so they cannot place themselves above the law they have sworn to uphold.

topics.title: Writing the Constitution of India
topics.summary: How a Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 to write the Constitution, who led it, the role of the Drafting Committee under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, and the key dates that gave us Republic Day.

concepts.title: The Constituent Assembly

explanations.oneLine: The Constituent Assembly was the elected body of representatives formed in 1946 to write India's Constitution.
explanations.kidFriendly: While India was still fighting for freedom, leaders began planning how the country would govern itself. To decide all the big questions — what kind of government, who can vote, how to settle disputes — a Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946. It started with 389 members (later 299 after Partition), and 15 of them were women. These members came from India's many regions, professions and social groups, so the Constitution would speak for everyone.
explanations.textbook: While India was struggling for independence from British rule, it became necessary to plan how the country would govern itself. To answer big questions — what type of government to have, what rules and principles should guide the country, who should have the right to vote, and how disputes should be decided — a Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946. It initially had 389 members, later reduced to 299 after the Partition of India, of which 15 were women. These members represented India's diverse regions, professions and social groups. The Assembly was formed on 9 December 1946, and its members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose own members had been elected by the people.
explanations.expert: A 'constituent' assembly is one specially charged with framing a constitution, exercising the founding (constituent) power of the people rather than the ordinary law-making power. India's Assembly was indirectly elected — chosen by the provincial legislative assemblies, themselves elected on a limited franchise — yet it deliberately sought representation across regions, religions, castes, professions and gender so that the document would carry broad legitimacy. Its reduction from 389 to 299 members reflects the trauma of Partition, when members from areas that became Pakistan withdrew. The deliberative method, nearly three years of debate clause by clause, gave the Constitution its character of reasoned consensus rather than imposition, a key reason it has endured.

concepts.reasoning: For a constitution to be accepted by a huge, diverse country, it cannot be written by one ruler — it must be made by people who represent the whole nation. So an assembly drawn from India's many regions, professions and communities was formed, giving the resulting document authority and acceptance across the country.

concepts.title: Dr. Rajendra Prasad and the Drafting Committee

explanations.oneLine: Dr. Rajendra Prasad chaired the Constituent Assembly, while a Drafting Committee headed by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar prepared the initial text.
explanations.kidFriendly: Writing the Constitution was teamwork. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the Chairman of the whole Constituent Assembly. To actually write the first text, a smaller group called the Drafting Committee was set up, led by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar — a great social reformer who became independent India's first Law and Justice minister.
explanations.textbook: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly. The initial text of the Constitution was prepared by a Drafting Committee chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, an eminent social reformer and the first Law and Justice minister of independent India. The Indian Constitution was developed and written by the Constituent Assembly over a period of almost three years, with the drafting work completed and adopted as the Constitution of India on 26 November 1949.
explanations.expert: The division of labour between the full Assembly and the Drafting Committee is standard constitution-making practice: a large representative body sets directions and debates, while a small expert committee turns decisions into precise legal text. Dr. Ambedkar, as Chairman of the Drafting Committee, shaped the language, structure and safeguards of the document, especially provisions on equality and against discrimination, reflecting his lifelong fight against caste injustice; he is widely regarded as the principal architect of the Constitution. Dr. Rajendra Prasad, presiding over the Assembly, steered nearly three years of deliberation to consensus. The committee's drafts were debated clause by clause, amended, and only then adopted, a process that combined expert craftsmanship with democratic scrutiny.

concepts.reasoning: A document as large and detailed as a constitution needs both broad debate and careful drafting. So the full Assembly, chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, debated and decided, while a small expert Drafting Committee under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar turned those decisions into precise legal wording.

concepts.title: Key Dates: From Adoption to Republic Day

explanations.oneLine: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950, which we celebrate as Republic Day.
explanations.kidFriendly: There are three dates to remember. The Constituent Assembly was formed on 9 December 1946. After almost three years of work, the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949. It finally came into effect on 26 January 1950 — and that is why every year on 26 January we celebrate Republic Day with the great parade at Kartavya Path in Delhi.
explanations.textbook: The Indian Constitution was developed and written by the Constituent Assembly, which was formed on 9 December 1946, over a period of almost three years. The drafting work was completed and the document was adopted as the Constitution of India on 26 November 1949. The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, which is why we celebrate this day every year as Republic Day. The day is marked by the Republic Day Parade, including the unfurling of the tricolour at Kartavya Path.
explanations.expert: The gap between adoption (26 November 1949) and commencement (26 January 1950) was deliberate and symbolic. The Indian National Congress had declared 'Purna Swaraj' (complete independence) on 26 January 1930, and that date was celebrated through the freedom movement as Independence Day; bringing the Constitution into force on 26 January 1950 honoured that earlier pledge. The two dates therefore mark distinct legal moments: 'adoption' is when the Constituent Assembly approved and signed the text, while 'commencement' is when it actually became the operative supreme law of the Republic, transforming India from a Dominion into a sovereign democratic republic with its own head of state.

concepts.reasoning: A constitution is first written and approved, then formally brought into force. India's Assembly adopted the text on 26 November 1949, but chose 26 January 1950 to enforce it, honouring the 1930 'complete independence' pledge — so Republic Day marks the day the Constitution actually became the law of the land.

topics.title: What Shaped the Indian Constitution
topics.summary: The three great influences on the Constitution — the ideals of the freedom struggle, India's own civilisational heritage, and useful learnings from the constitutions of other countries.

concepts.title: Influence of the Freedom Movement

explanations.oneLine: The ideals and experiences of India's freedom struggle were carried into the Constitution by leaders who had fought for independence.
explanations.kidFriendly: Many of the people who fought for India's freedom were also members of the Constituent Assembly. So the dreams of the freedom struggle — equality for all, justice for all, freedom and fraternity — were written straight into the Constitution. The struggle had also taught India practical lessons, like how to make sure every adult could vote and how to keep the parts of government separate.
explanations.textbook: Many key ideals and values of the Indian freedom struggle were enshrined in the Constitution, which became the cornerstone for an independent India. A number of leaders of the freedom movement were members of the Constituent Assembly and carried their experience and ideas from the struggle into the Constitution. Some of these values and ideals are: equality of all, justice for all, freedom, fraternity, and the preservation of India's cultural heritage. The experience of the freedom struggle also helped answer practical 'how' and 'what' questions, such as how to ensure every adult citizen has the right to vote, how to keep the powers of the executive, legislature and judiciary separate, how to guarantee fundamental rights, how the Constitution could be amended, and what the relationship between the Central and State governments should be.
explanations.expert: The freedom movement functioned as a long political laboratory whose conclusions hardened into constitutional choices. Decades of mass mobilisation across castes, religions and regions made universal adult franchise an obvious commitment — remarkably, India adopted 'one person, one vote' from the very start, unlike many older democracies that extended the vote only gradually. The movement's insistence on civil liberties under colonial repression shaped the chapter on Fundamental Rights; its experience of arbitrary executive power shaped the demand for an independent judiciary and separation of powers; and its negotiation of India's plurality shaped federalism and minority safeguards. The Constitution thus reads, in part, as the codified memory of the freedom struggle's hard-won lessons.

concepts.reasoning: The people who wrote the Constitution had just lived through the freedom struggle, so its lessons were fresh in their minds. The ideals they had fought for — equality, justice, freedom, fraternity — became the Constitution's values, and the problems they had faced under colonial rule shaped practical rules like the right to vote and separation of powers.

concepts.title: Influence of India's Civilisational Heritage

explanations.oneLine: Age-old Indian values like respect for differing views, the idea of duties, and 'the world is one family' shaped the Constitution.
explanations.kidFriendly: The Constitution did not appear from nowhere — many of its ideas come from India's own ancient culture. Old Indian traditions valued accepting that people can have different views, treating Nature as sacred, the pursuit of knowledge, and respect for women. Beautiful ideas like vasudhaiva kutumbakam ('the world is one family') and a strong sense of people's duties all found a place in the Constitution, even if expressed in modern words.
explanations.textbook: India's civilisational heritage and culture played a key role in shaping the Constitution. Some fundamental principles are embedded in Indian culture — the acceptance that people could have different points of view, treating Nature as sacred, the pursuit of learning and knowledge, respect for women, and the concepts of vasudhaiva kutumbakam ('the world is one family') and sarve bhavantu sukhinah (an invocation for the well-being of all creatures). All these principles find a place in the Constitution, though they may be expressed a little differently. India had also experimented with many governance systems — janapadas, sanghas, rulers and their councils, and ideas like Kauṭilya's saptanga and rajadharma — with a great emphasis on the duties and role of the people. So it was natural for the Constitution-makers to include such ideas, and 'Fundamental Duties', for instance, are part of the Constitution.
explanations.expert: This influence is one of substance, not just sentiment. India's long tradition of pluralism — the acceptance of many viewpoints, sects and ways of life — underlies the constitutional commitments to secularism and to protecting diversity, captured by the older idea of 'unity in diversity'. The traditional stress on dharma and on the duties of rulers (rajadharma) and people anticipates the Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A). Pre-modern political experimentation — republican sanghas and janapadas, councils advising rulers, Kauṭilya's saptanga (the seven limbs of the state) — shows that consultative and rule-bound governance was not imported wholesale but resonated with indigenous practice. The Constitution-makers therefore drew on a civilisational vocabulary, re-expressed in modern legal form, which helped the document feel rooted rather than foreign.

concepts.reasoning: A constitution works best when it feels rooted in a country's own values. India already had deep traditions of accepting many viewpoints, respecting Nature and knowledge, and stressing people's duties — so the Constitution-makers wove these familiar ideas into the document, making it both modern and genuinely Indian.

concepts.title: Learnings from Other Countries

explanations.oneLine: India studied other democratic constitutions and borrowed useful ideas, like liberty-equality-fraternity from France and the independent judiciary idea from the USA.
explanations.kidFriendly: In the spirit of the old saying 'Let noble thoughts come to me from every side', the Constitution-makers studied other countries' constitutions to find good ideas. From France's revolution came the famous values of liberty, equality and fraternity. The idea of an independent judiciary (courts free from government control) was shaped by the American Constitution, and the Directive Principles of State Policy were inspired by Ireland's Constitution.
explanations.textbook: The Constitution-makers, in the Indian tradition of 'a no bhadrah kratavo yantu vishwatah' ('Let noble thoughts come to me from every side'), studied the constitutions of France, the USA, the UK, Ireland, Australia and other countries with a democratic system, to explore their usefulness for India's context. For example, the ideals of 'liberty, equality, fraternity' were adopted from France's constitution, which had enshrined them from the French Revolution of 1789; the idea of the Directive Principles of State Policy was inspired by the Irish Constitution; and the American Constitution helped shape the concept of an independent judiciary.
explanations.expert: Comparative borrowing was selective and adaptive rather than imitative. From Britain India took the parliamentary (Westminster) form of government and the rule of law; from the United States, judicial review and an independent judiciary (and the very idea of a written, supreme Constitution with a Bill of Rights); from Ireland, the non-justiciable Directive Principles of State Policy as a statement of social goals; from France, the revolutionary trio of liberty, equality and fraternity; and from Australia, ideas about the federal arrangement and Concurrent List. The framers fitted each borrowed element to Indian conditions, producing a hybrid that is parliamentary like Britain yet federal and rights-protecting like the USA — an example of constitutional learning across borders.

concepts.reasoning: There was no need for India to invent everything from scratch. By studying democratic constitutions that had worked elsewhere, the makers could adopt tested ideas — but they adapted each one to India's own needs, rather than copying blindly.

topics.title: Key Features of the Constitution
topics.summary: The three organs of government and separation of powers, the Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles of State Policy, and why the Constitution is a 'living document' that can be amended.

concepts.title: Three Organs and Separation of Powers

explanations.oneLine: The Constitution sets up three organs of government — legislature, executive and judiciary — and keeps their powers separate.
explanations.kidFriendly: The Constitution divides the government into three parts so that no single part becomes too powerful. The legislature makes the laws. The executive, headed by the Prime Minister, carries out the laws. The judiciary (the courts) checks that all laws follow the Constitution and decides whether a law has been broken. India also has a three-tier system — central, state and local (Panchayati Raj) — so power is shared at every level.
explanations.textbook: There are three organs of government — the legislature, the executive and the judiciary — and the 'separation of powers' among them is essential for their effective working. The legislature makes the laws. The law is implemented by the executive, which is headed by the Prime Minister. The judiciary ensures that all laws made are in accordance with the Constitution, and also decides whether a law has been broken and what punishment is necessary. India has a three-tier system of government — central, state and local (the Panchayati Raj system). Some functions and responsibilities are reserved for the central government and others are assigned to the state government. The Constitution clearly defines the roles, functions, responsibilities and accountability of each organ, and lays down an electoral system so that every eligible citizen can vote.
explanations.expert: Separation of powers distributes the three core state functions — making, executing and interpreting law — among distinct organs so that each can check the others, preventing the concentration of power that leads to tyranny. India follows a parliamentary version in which the executive (the council of ministers) is drawn from and accountable to the legislature, so the separation is functional rather than rigid, but the judiciary stands genuinely independent and exercises judicial review. Layered on top is a federal, three-tier structure (Union, State, and local self-government), with subjects divided through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists. The result is a double dispersal of power — horizontally across organs and vertically across levels — which is the structural heart of Indian constitutionalism.

concepts.reasoning: If one body could make laws, enforce them and judge disputes, it could do whatever it liked. Splitting these jobs among three organs lets each watch the others, so power is checked. Sharing power across central, state and local levels spreads it further still.

concepts.title: Rights, Duties and Directive Principles

explanations.oneLine: The Constitution gives citizens Fundamental Rights (enforceable promises), Fundamental Duties (responsibilities), and Directive Principles (goals for the government).
explanations.kidFriendly: The Constitution has three special sets of rules for citizens and government. Fundamental Rights are promises that MUST be kept — if someone treats you unfairly, you can go to court. Fundamental Duties are the responsibilities of every citizen, like respecting the flag and protecting the environment. Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are big goals the government should try to reach, like a good standard of living for all — but you cannot take the government to court if it does not achieve them; they are more like guidelines.
explanations.textbook: Three core aspects of the Constitution are the Fundamental Rights, the Fundamental Duties and the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). Fundamental Rights — such as the Right to Equality (Article 14), the Right to Freedom (Article 21), the Right against Exploitation and the Right to Education (Article 21-A) — are promises that must be kept: if someone treats you unfairly because of who you are, you can go to court and a judge can help you. Fundamental Duties are the responsibilities of citizens, such as to abide by the Constitution, respect the National Flag and National Anthem, defend the country, value the rich heritage of our composite culture, and protect the natural environment. The Directive Principles of State Policy represent the social and economic vision the framers had for India — for example, a good standard of living for everyone — but they are guidelines rather than strict rules, so one cannot go to a judge to complain if the government does not follow them.
explanations.expert: These three components are deliberately different in legal force. Fundamental Rights (Part III) are 'justiciable' — citizens can move the courts directly to enforce them, and laws violating them can be struck down; they create a sphere the state may not invade. The Directive Principles (Part IV) are 'non-justiciable' — they are not enforceable in court but are 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and guide policy and legislation toward social and economic justice. Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) are obligations on citizens, not on the state. The framers chose this design on purpose: rights that could be demanded immediately, paired with larger goals that a developing nation would realise gradually, balancing individual liberty against the collective project of building a just society.

concepts.reasoning: A good constitution must protect individuals now and also point the country toward a better future. So it makes Fundamental Rights enforceable at once, sets out Fundamental Duties that citizens owe in return, and lists Directive Principles as longer-term goals that a developing country can work toward over time.

whyChain: Why does the Constitution separate Fundamental Rights from Directive Principles? Because the two do different jobs. Fundamental Rights protect each individual right now — they are promises that must be kept, so if someone is treated unfairly they can go straight to court and a judge can act. Directive Principles, by contrast, set out big social and economic goals for the whole nation, like a good standard of living for everyone, which a young, developing country cannot achieve overnight but must keep working toward.

Why are Directive Principles only guidelines and not enforceable in court? Because goals like ending poverty or ensuring good health for all depend on resources, time and steady effort that the country has to build up gradually. If citizens could sue the government for not yet achieving them, courts would be deciding budgets and priorities that belong to elected governments. So the framers made the Principles 'fundamental in governance' to guide policy, but left their pace to the democratic process, while keeping Rights immediately enforceable.

Why pair rights with Fundamental Duties? Because a society where people only demand rights but accept no responsibilities cannot function fairly. The duties — to respect the flag and anthem, protect the environment, value our composite culture, defend the country and educate one's children — remind citizens that the freedoms the Constitution guarantees are sustained only when each person also contributes. Rights and duties together express the balance the Constitution-makers, drawing on India's heritage, wanted between the individual and the community.

concepts.title: A Living Document

explanations.oneLine: The Constitution is a 'living document' because it can be changed by amendments as the country's needs evolve.
explanations.kidFriendly: The makers of the Constitution knew that India would change over time and would need new rules. So they made it a 'living document' that can be updated through changes called amendments. For example, the Fundamental Duties were added in 1976, and the Panchayati Raj system was added in 1992. But amendments are not made carelessly — they are rigorously debated in Parliament, and sometimes in state assemblies and with the public, before being accepted.
explanations.textbook: The Constitution is a living document. Its makers realised that a need for new laws and rules would emerge over time. For example, 'Part IV-A: Fundamental Duties' was added in 1976, and the Panchayati Raj system — which was not part of the original Constitution — was integrated into it in 1992 through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act. Any changes, called amendments, are rigorously debated in Parliament before they are accepted; some require a debate in legislative assemblies as well, opinions are often sought from the general public, and some changes can even be initiated by popular movements. For instance, after a citizen challenged a rule in court in 2004, the Supreme Court held that flying the national flag is part of the Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression, so citizens may now fly the tricolour with pride.
explanations.expert: Calling the Constitution a 'living document' captures both its formal amendability and its evolving interpretation. Formally, Article 368 lays down amendment procedures requiring special majorities in Parliament, with certain federal provisions also needing ratification by half the state legislatures — a process more demanding than ordinary law-making, which protects the Constitution's supremacy while allowing change. Substantively, the document also lives through judicial interpretation: courts read its words in light of new circumstances, as when the Supreme Court located the right to fly the flag within freedom of expression. This adaptability is balanced by limits — the 'basic structure' doctrine holds that the fundamental framework cannot be amended away — so the Constitution can grow without losing its essential identity.

concepts.reasoning: No one can foresee every future need, so a constitution that could never change would soon become outdated and useless. Making it a living document, changeable by carefully debated amendments, lets it adapt to new situations while still protecting its core through demanding procedures.

So Rights can be demanded immediately, while Directive Principles are bigger goals to be reached over time.

topics.title: Understanding the Preamble
topics.summary: The Preamble as the heart of the Constitution, its description of India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic, and the goals it sets out — Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.

concepts.title: The Preamble and 'We, the People'

explanations.oneLine: The Preamble is the opening statement of the Constitution that sums up its core guiding values.
explanations.kidFriendly: The Preamble is like the introduction at the very start of the Constitution. In just a few lines it captures all the most important values the country stands for. It begins with the powerful words 'WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA', which means the Constitution was drawn up and given to the country by the people themselves, through their representatives — not handed down by a king or any outside power.
explanations.textbook: The Constitution's core values are the guiding principles for policies and decision-making, which the government is expected to follow and which citizens are also expected to practise to the best of their ability. These guiding values are present across the whole Constitution, but their essence is written in the Preamble. The Preamble opens with the words 'WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA', showing that the Constitution has been drawn up and enacted by the people through their representatives, and not handed down to them by a king or any outside power. It then describes the kind of nation India is — a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic — and the goals it seeks to secure for all citizens: Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
explanations.expert: The Preamble functions as the Constitution's mission statement and interpretive key. The phrase 'We, the People of India' asserts popular sovereignty — that ultimate authority rests with the people, who are the source of the Constitution's legitimacy. Although the Preamble itself is not directly enforceable, courts treat it as a guide to the Constitution's spirit and have held it to be part of the basic structure, using it to resolve ambiguities. It compactly states the nature of the polity (the four adjectives describing the Republic) and its aims (the four goals). Studying it last, as this chapter does, is apt: it gathers into a few lines the values that the rest of the document works out in detail.

concepts.reasoning: A long, detailed document needs a short statement of what it is all about. The Preamble does this by declaring who made the Constitution (the people), what kind of country India is, and what goals it pursues — so it acts as the heart and summary of the whole Constitution.

concepts.title: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic

explanations.oneLine: The Preamble describes India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic — five words that define what kind of nation India is.
explanations.kidFriendly: Five big words in the Preamble describe India. Sovereign: India makes its own decisions and no outside power can dictate to it. Socialist: wealth is created by society and should be shared, with the government reducing the gap between rich and poor. Secular: citizens are free to follow any religion and there is no official state religion. Democratic: the people elect their leaders and can hold them accountable. Republic: the head of state (the President) is elected, not a king who inherits the throne.
explanations.textbook: The Preamble describes India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. SOVEREIGN means the people have the supreme right to make decisions on internal as well as external matters, and no external power can dictate the government of India. SOCIALIST means wealth is generated socially and should be shared by society, and the government should regulate the ownership of land and industry to reduce socio-economic inequalities. SECULAR means citizens have complete freedom to follow any religion, but there is no official religion and the government treats all religious beliefs and practices with equal respect. DEMOCRATIC means a form of government where the people enjoy equal political rights, elect their rulers and hold them accountable, and the government is run according to some basic rules. REPUBLIC means the head of the state is an elected person and not a hereditary position. The terms 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in 1976.
explanations.expert: Each term is a precise constitutional concept. Sovereignty means supreme legal authority, internal and external, with no superior power — India is bound by no foreign government. Socialist signals a commitment to social and economic justice and the reduction of inequality, pursued through democratic means rather than state ownership of everything. Secularism, in the Indian sense, is not hostility to religion but equal respect for all faiths with no state religion — a model suited to India's deep religious plurality. Democratic denotes government by the people through periodic, equal elections and accountability of rulers. Republic means the head of state is elected, not hereditary, marking the final break from monarchy and colonial rule. That 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were inserted only in 1976 (42nd Amendment) shows the Preamble itself is part of the Constitution's living, amendable text.

concepts.reasoning: These five words are not decoration — each makes a definite claim about India. Together they say India answers to no foreign power, works to reduce inequality, respects all religions equally, is run by the people through elections, and has an elected (not hereditary) head of state.

concepts.title: Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity

explanations.oneLine: The Preamble promises every citizen Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity — the four goals the Constitution seeks to secure.
explanations.kidFriendly: Besides describing India, the Preamble lists four goals for everyone. JUSTICE: no one can be discriminated against because of caste, religion or gender, and social inequalities must be reduced. LIBERTY: there are no unreasonable restrictions on what citizens think, how they express themselves, and how they act. EQUALITY: all are equal before the law, social inequalities must end, and the government must ensure equal opportunity for all. FRATERNITY: we should all behave as members of one family, and no one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior.
explanations.textbook: The Preamble sets out four goals for all citizens. JUSTICE means citizens cannot be discriminated against on the grounds of caste, religion or gender; social inequalities have to be reduced; and the government should work for the welfare of all, especially of less advantaged groups. LIBERTY means there are no unreasonable restrictions on citizens in what they think, how they wish to express their thoughts, and the way they wish to follow up their thoughts in action. EQUALITY means all are equal before the law, social inequalities have to be ended, and the government should ensure equal opportunity for all. FRATERNITY means all of us should behave as if we are members of the same family, and no one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior.
explanations.expert: These four goals are mutually reinforcing and were drawn, in part, from the French Revolution's 'liberty, equality, fraternity', with justice added at the head. Justice spans the social, economic and political; liberty protects freedom of thought, expression, belief and action against arbitrary restriction; equality combines formal equality (equality before the law) with substantive equality (ending entrenched social inequalities and ensuring equal opportunity). Fraternity, often the least discussed, is the cement: it asks citizens to see one another as members of one family, sustaining the dignity of the individual and the unity of the nation. The framers understood that liberty without equality breeds privilege, and equality without liberty breeds coercion, while fraternity is needed for both to survive — a balance that defines the Indian constitutional vision.

concepts.reasoning: A nation needs not just a structure of government but goals to strive for. Justice, liberty, equality and fraternity spell out what the Constitution wants for every citizen — fair treatment, freedom, equal standing, and a sense of belonging together — so they act as the country's shared aims.

solutionSteps: Recall what 'We, the People of India' means.

realWorldExamples.title: The kabaddi rulebook
realWorldExamples.body: Imagine your school's kabaddi team in a state-level final. A player gets an opponent 'out', but the other team disputes it. To settle the argument fairly, the referee pulls out a little official rulebook that both teams have agreed to follow. They check the rules, agree the player was 'out', and your team wins — peacefully. A constitution is exactly this kind of rulebook, but for a whole country: because everyone accepts it in advance, disputes about power and rights can be settled fairly instead of by force.

realWorldExamples.title: Flying the tricolour with pride
realWorldExamples.body: There was a time when people in India were not allowed to fly the national flag at their homes. In 2004 a citizen felt that expressing pride in his country was his right and challenged the rule in court. The Supreme Court agreed, holding that flying the flag is part of the Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression. Now any citizen can fly the tricolour with pride (keeping in mind it must never be dishonoured) — a perfect example of how the Constitution is a 'living document' that grows through the courts.

realWorldExamples.title: The Constitution kept in helium
realWorldExamples.body: The original handwritten Constitution of India is so precious that it is stored in a special airtight glass case in Parliament, filled with helium gas. Helium does not react with paper or ink, so it slows the natural ageing and decay of the historic document, keeping it safe for future generations. It is a striking reminder of how much value the country places on its founding rulebook.

mnemonics.unpacking: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic — the five words in the Preamble that describe India. Remember them as 'Some Strong Students Don't Rest'.

misconceptions.kidsThink: 'Secular' means India is against religion or has no religion.
misconceptions.actually: 'Secular' means citizens have complete freedom to follow ANY religion, that there is no official state religion, and that the government treats all religious beliefs and practices with equal respect. It is about equal respect for all faiths, not opposition to religion.

misconceptions.kidsThink: The Constitution can never be changed once it was written.
misconceptions.actually: The Constitution is a 'living document' that can be changed through amendments as the country's needs evolve — for example, Fundamental Duties were added in 1976 and Panchayati Raj in 1992. But amendments are rigorously debated before being accepted.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Republic Day (26 January) is when India became independent.
misconceptions.actually: India became independent on 15 August 1947 (Independence Day). Republic Day, 26 January, marks the day the Constitution came into effect in 1950, turning India into a republic with its own supreme rulebook.

ncertQA.question: 'The Constituent Assembly had representatives from diverse backgrounds in India.' Why do you think it was important to have a diverse set of representatives from all over India?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: It was important because India is a very large and culturally diverse country, with people of many regions, religions, castes, languages and professions. If the Constitution had been written only by one group, it would have reflected only their interests and might have been rejected by others. By including representatives from diverse backgrounds — different regions, professions and social groups, and 15 women — the Constituent Assembly made sure that the concerns of many different communities were heard and built into the Constitution. This gave the document wide acceptance and legitimacy, so people across the whole country could feel it was truly their own rulebook.

ncertQA.question: Read the statements and identify which key feature or value of the Constitution is reflected: (a) Sheena, Rajat and Harsh are excited to cast their first vote in the general elections. (b) Radha, Imon and Harpreet study in the same class in the same school. (c) Parents must make arrangements to ensure their children's education. (d) People of all castes, genders and religions can use the village well.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: (a) The right to vote in elections reflects DEMOCRACY (and universal adult franchise) — the people elect their rulers. (b) Children of different backgrounds studying together reflects EQUALITY and the Right to Education (Article 21-A). (c) Parents ensuring their children's education reflects a FUNDAMENTAL DUTY (and supports the Right to Education). (d) People of all castes, genders and religions using the same well reflects EQUALITY and JUSTICE — no discrimination on grounds of caste, religion or gender.

ncertQA.question: You have learnt that 'India is the only country that provided universal adult franchise to its citizens from the beginning.' Can you explain why India did it?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: India provided universal adult franchise — the right of every adult to vote, regardless of wealth, education, caste, religion or gender — from its very first election. India did this because the freedom struggle had been a mass movement involving people from every section of society, who had fought together for independence and self-rule. It would have been unfair to then deny any of them a say in choosing their government. The Constitution-makers believed in equality and justice for all, and trusted the ordinary people of India. By contrast, many older democracies had given the vote only gradually, first to wealthy or educated men and only much later to women and the poor. India's bold decision showed deep faith in democracy and in the equality of all its citizens.

ncertQA.question: How did the freedom struggle inspire the making of the Constitution of India? How did India's civilisational heritage inspire some of the key features in the Constitution? Explain.
ncertQA.modelAnswer: The freedom struggle inspired the Constitution in two ways. First, the ideals the freedom fighters had fought for — equality of all, justice for all, freedom, fraternity and preservation of India's cultural heritage — were written into the Constitution, because many freedom-movement leaders were themselves members of the Constituent Assembly. Second, the experience of the struggle answered practical questions, such as giving every adult the right to vote, keeping the powers of the executive, legislature and judiciary separate, and guaranteeing fundamental rights. India's civilisational heritage inspired key features too: the old acceptance of different points of view supports secularism and pluralism; respect for Nature and the well-being of all creatures appears in values like sarve bhavantu sukhinah; and the long tradition stressing the duties of people (seen in janapadas, sanghas, rajadharma and Kauṭilya's saptanga) inspired the inclusion of Fundamental Duties.

glossary.definition: The supreme document that spells out a nation's basic principles and laws, setting up the government, the rights and duties of citizens, and the country's long-term goals.
glossary.example: The Constitution of India came into effect on 26 January 1950.

glossary.definition: The body of elected representatives formed in 1946 to write the Constitution of India.
glossary.example: The Constituent Assembly had 389 members, later reduced to 299 after Partition.

glossary.definition: The opening statement of the Constitution that sums up its core guiding values and the kind of nation India is.
glossary.example: The Preamble begins with the words 'We, the People of India'.

glossary.definition: Having the supreme right to make decisions on internal and external matters, with no external power able to dictate the government.
glossary.example: India is a sovereign nation that makes its own foreign policy.

glossary.definition: Allowing citizens complete freedom to follow any religion, with no official state religion and equal respect for all faiths.
glossary.example: Because India is secular, the State has no official religion.

glossary.definition: A form of state in which the head of state is an elected person, not a hereditary king or queen.
glossary.example: India is a republic with an elected President as head of state.

glossary.definition: Basic rights guaranteed to citizens that must be protected, and which can be enforced through the courts.
glossary.example: The Right to Equality and the Right to Freedom are Fundamental Rights.

glossary.definition: The responsibilities of citizens listed in the Constitution, such as respecting the National Flag and protecting the environment.
glossary.example: Protecting forests, lakes and rivers is a Fundamental Duty.

glossary.definition: Goals and guidelines for the government to work toward, which cannot be enforced in court but guide its policies.
glossary.example: Ensuring a good standard of living for all is a Directive Principle.

glossary.definition: A change made to the Constitution, rigorously debated in Parliament before it is accepted.
glossary.example: Fundamental Duties were added by an amendment in 1976.

miniProjects.title: Design a class constitution
steps: As a class, brainstorm what problems or disputes commonly arise in your classroom (turns, sharing, cleaning, noise).
Collect everyone's suggested rules in the suggestion box, so every student gets a voice — like a Constituent Assembly.
Read out the suggestions and discuss them; group similar ones together.
Write a short Preamble beginning 'We, the students of Class 7…' stating your class's shared values.
List a few 'rights' (e.g., the right to be heard) and matching 'duties' (e.g., the duty to keep the room clean).
Add a rule for how the class constitution itself can be changed later (your own 'amendment' process).
Vote to adopt the class constitution, then display it on the wall.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: You will see how hard but how fair it is to agree on rules everyone accepts, and why a constitution needs both rights and duties plus a way to be amended.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: Building rules together by discussion and voting mirrors exactly how the Constituent Assembly worked, turning the abstract idea of a constitution into a real, lived experience of consensus, rights, duties and amendment.

miniProjects.title: Hunt for the Constitution in daily life
steps: For one week, watch out for moments in your neighbourhood that show a Preamble value in action.
Write down anything that shows EQUALITY (e.g., people of all castes using the same well or bus).
Write down anything that shows LIBERTY (e.g., people freely expressing opinions or following their religion).
Write down anything that shows JUSTICE (e.g., equal treatment regardless of gender or background).
Note any moment showing FRATERNITY (people helping each other as one community).
For each observation, write which Preamble word it matches and one line on why.
Share your list with the class and compare findings.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: You will discover that the values written in the Preamble are not just words in a book — they show up in ordinary, everyday life all around you.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: Linking abstract constitutional values to concrete daily scenes makes them memorable and real, and trains you to 'read' society through the lens of the Constitution's ideals.

whatIfs.question: What if India had no constitution at all?
whatIfs.answer: Without a constitution, there would be no agreed rulebook to say who governs, how power is limited, or what rights people have. Disputes would be settled by whoever was strongest, not by fair rules, and rulers could do whatever they liked because nothing would bind them. There would be no clear way to make laws, hold elections, or protect citizens who are treated unfairly, and a huge, diverse country like India could easily fall into confusion and conflict. The constitution is what lets such a varied nation be governed fairly and stay united.

whatIfs.question: What if the Constitution could never be amended?
whatIfs.answer: If the Constitution could never change, it would slowly become outdated as the country's needs evolved. New ideas and bodies that were not thought of in 1950 — like the Fundamental Duties added in 1976 or the Panchayati Raj system added in 1992 — could never have been included. The Constitution might no longer fit modern India, and people would either have to ignore it or scrap it and start again. By making it a 'living document' that can be carefully amended after rigorous debate, the makers let it grow with the country while keeping its core values safe.

timelines.title: Making the Constitution of India, 1946–1950
timelines.intro: The key milestones in how India's Constitution was written and brought into force.

steps.label: Constituent Assembly formed
steps.body: On 9 December 1946, the Constituent Assembly is formed to write India's Constitution, initially with 389 members.

steps.label: Partition reduces members
steps.body: After the Partition of India in 1947, the Assembly's membership is reduced to 299, of which 15 are women.

steps.label: Drafting Committee at work
steps.body: A Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, prepares the initial text while Dr. Rajendra Prasad chairs the full Assembly.
steps.assetHint: drafting committee members at a table

steps.label: Constitution adopted
steps.body: After almost three years of debate, the Constitution of India is adopted on 26 November 1949 (now Constitution Day).

steps.label: Constitution comes into effect
steps.body: On 26 January 1950 the Constitution comes into effect, making India a republic — celebrated every year as Republic Day.

examConnections.title: The Constitution returns in higher classes
examConnections.body: The ideas introduced here — the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, separation of powers and the federal structure — are studied in much greater depth in Class 8 ('The Indian Constitution', 'Understanding Secularism') and again in Class 9–10 Political Science (Democratic Politics). The making of the Constitution and the Constituent Assembly are favourite topics in board exams. Mastering the basics now — key dates, who chaired what, and the meaning of the Preamble words — makes the advanced version far easier later.

examConnections.title: Polity in competitive exams
examConnections.body: Indian Polity is one of the most heavily tested subjects in competitive and civil-services examinations. Examiners love the exact facts of this chapter: the Constituent Assembly's formation (9 December 1946), Dr. Ambedkar as Drafting Committee chairman, adoption on 26 November 1949, commencement on 26 January 1950, the sources borrowed from other countries (France, Ireland, USA), and the 42nd Amendment adding 'Socialist' and 'Secular' in 1976. Knowing these precisely gives a strong head start.

deepDive.title: Why the Directive Principles can't be enforced in court
deepDive.body: Fundamental Rights are 'justiciable' — you can take a violation straight to court and a judge can order the government to act. Directive Principles are 'non-justiciable' — they cannot be enforced in court. Why the difference? Goals like ending poverty, ensuring good health and a decent standard of living for everyone need money, time and steady effort that a developing country has to build up gradually. If anyone could sue the government for not yet achieving them, judges, rather than elected governments, would end up deciding budgets and priorities. So the framers made the Directive Principles 'fundamental in the governance of the country' to guide policy, while leaving the pace of achieving them to the democratic process — and kept Fundamental Rights immediately enforceable so individuals are protected right now.
deepDive.prerequisite: Knowing that Fundamental Rights can be enforced in court but Directive Principles are guidelines.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Find one government scheme (for health, food or education) that puts a Directive Principle into action.

deepDive.title: The 'basic structure' — limits on amendment
deepDive.body: The Constitution is a living document that can be amended, but can Parliament change anything at all, even its core values? In a famous 1973 case (Kesavananda Bharati), the Supreme Court answered: no. It held that while Parliament can amend the Constitution, it cannot destroy or alter its 'basic structure' — features like the supremacy of the Constitution, democracy, secularism, separation of powers, the rule of law and judicial review. This doctrine is the reason the Constitution can grow with the country yet never lose its essential identity. It is a brilliant balance: flexible enough to adapt, but protected against being twisted into something that is no longer a free, democratic constitution.
deepDive.prerequisite: Understanding that the Constitution can be changed through amendments under a special procedure.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Read what the 'basic structure doctrine' lists as features that cannot be amended away.

A list of the country's festivals
A map of the country's borders

It sets out basic principles and laws, government, rights and duties.
Choose that option.
commonMistakes: Confusing a constitution with a history book.

bossQuestions.prompt: The Constituent Assembly that wrote the Constitution was formed in —
solutionSteps: Recall the Assembly was formed on 9 December 1946.
Choose 1946.

bossQuestions.prompt: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
solutionSteps: Recall the Drafting Committee wrote the initial text.
It was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
Choose Ambedkar.
commonMistakes: Confusing the Assembly's Chairman (Dr. Rajendra Prasad) with the Drafting Committee's chairman.

bossQuestions.prompt: The Constitution of India came into effect on —
solutionSteps: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.
It came into effect on 26 January 1950 — Republic Day.
Choose 26 January 1950.
commonMistakes: Choosing 15 August 1947 (Independence Day) or 26 November 1949 (adoption date).

bossQuestions.prompt: Which organ of government makes the laws?
solutionSteps: Recall the three organs.
The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them, the judiciary interprets them.
Choose the legislature.
commonMistakes: Confusing the executive (implements) with the legislature (makes laws).

bossQuestions.prompt: Which of these can you enforce by going to court if it is violated?
options: A Directive Principle of State Policy
A long-term goal of the nation
solutionSteps: Fundamental Rights are promises that must be kept and are enforceable in court.
Directive Principles are guidelines and cannot be enforced.
Choose Fundamental Right.
commonMistakes: Thinking Directive Principles can be enforced in court — they cannot.

bossQuestions.prompt: From which country's constitution did India adopt the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity?
solutionSteps: These ideals came from the French Revolution of 1789.
India adopted them from France's constitution.
Choose France.
commonMistakes: Confusing France (the three ideals) with the USA (independent judiciary).

bossQuestions.prompt: The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble by which amendment?
options: They were in the original Preamble
solutionSteps: Recall the note in the chapter.
'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
Choose that option.
commonMistakes: Thinking these words were in the original 1950 Preamble.

options: The head of state is an elected person, not hereditary
Wealth must be shared by society
bossQuestions.answer: The head of state is an elected person, not hereditary
solutionSteps: Recall the meaning of Republic in the chapter.
It means the head of state is elected, not a hereditary king.
Choose that option.
commonMistakes: Confusing 'Republic' (elected head of state) with 'Democratic' (people elect rulers) or 'Secular' (no official religion).

bossQuestions.prompt: The Constitution is called a 'living document' because —
options: It is read aloud every day
It can be changed through amendments as needs evolve
It is kept in a glass case
It was written by living people
bossQuestions.answer: It can be changed through amendments as needs evolve
solutionSteps: Recall that a living document can change over time.
It changes through amendments, like adding Fundamental Duties (1976).
Choose that option.
commonMistakes: Thinking 'living document' refers to how it is stored or read.

quickCheckQuestions.prompt: On which day every year do we celebrate the Constitution coming into effect?
solutionSteps: The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950.
We celebrate this as Republic Day.
Choose 26 January.
commonMistakes: Choosing Independence Day (15 August) instead of Republic Day.

quickCheckQuestions.prompt: The opening words of the Preamble are —
solutionSteps: Recall the Preamble's opening.
It begins 'WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA'.
Choose that option.
commonMistakes: Thinking it begins with 'the Government' or 'the President'.

quickCheckQuestions.prompt: Citizens of all castes, genders and religions using the same village well best reflects which Preamble values?
solutionSteps: Equal use regardless of caste, gender or religion shows Equality.
No discrimination on these grounds shows Justice.
Choose Equality and Justice.
